content.text: {"relation":"DIVERGENT","consensus_summary":"All three blind responses identify the ship primarily as the Church — the vessel of salvation carrying believers through the sea of the world toward eternal safety, rooted in patristic tradition (barque of Peter, nave, Noah's ark typology) and the Gospel storm narratives. Secondary meanings include the individual life-voyage of faith and, as a context-dependent alternative, worldly commerce/wealth/pride (ships of Tarshish, Tyre in Ezekiel 27, Babylon in Revelation 18).","book_summary":"The book identifies the ship as an earthly kingdom, city, state, or governed political body riding upon the sea of peoples: rulers as pilots, inhabitants as crew, armies as defenders, wealth as cargo. It explicitly denies that Christ needs any constructed vessel — He walks on the sea directly — and holds that when He sails with the disciples the vessel merely comes under its true Head. The ship may be destroyed while its people survive.","consensus_core_identification":"Ship = the Church, the corporate vessel of salvation preserving believers through the world's dangers.","book_core_identification":"Ship = an earthly kingdom, city, or governed political body (a human polity moving upon the sea of peoples), emphatically not a body Christ requires.","core_relation":"CONTRADICTS","extension_relation":"PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION","boundary_disagreement":"The book retains the cases the consensus treats as a secondary alternative (Tyre in Ezekiel 27, ships of Tarshish in Isaiah 23, Babylon's shipping in Revelation 18, Paul's literal ship in Acts 27, Jonah's ship) and elevates them to the definition, while excluding or reinterpreting the cases central to the consensus: the disciples' boat is no longer the Church but a vessel that merely 'comes under its true Head' when Christ boards it, and Noah's ark/1 Peter 3 typology is absent from the book's basis entirely.","material_contradiction":"The consensus says the ship IS the Church, the vehicle of salvation with Christ as pilot. The book says the ship is an earthly political body and that 'Christ needs no constructed body beneath Him' — a direct rejection of the ecclesial identification, since a kingdom-of-this-world that Christ does not need cannot simultaneously be the Church He founded and preserves. Accepting the book requires rejecting the consensus's central referent.","rationale":"Both readings cannot be true of the same symbol in the same sense: the consensus makes the ship the divinely commissioned corporate body of believers; the book makes it a human political construct, explicitly denying Christ any dependence on it and noting it may be broken while its people survive (Acts 27) — a fate incompatible with the Church-as-ark of preservation. The book's referent overlaps with the consensus's listed 'worldly commerce/pride' alternative, but that alternative is framed by the consensus as commerce and wealth, whereas the book generalizes to any governed polity and installs it as the sole primary meaning while displacing the Church reading. This is replacement of the central identification, not boundary refinement, though the extension is a partial reclassification since Tyre/Babylon cases are shared.","citation_support":"STRONG","strongest_objection":"The book's meaning is arguably anticipated by the consensus alternatives — Ezekiel 27's Tyre-as-ship and Revelation 18's Babylon are explicitly listed as a common/minority reading in all three responses — so one could argue the book merely promotes a recognized alternative to primary status, which would suggest REFINED rather than DIVERGENT. However, the book does more than reweight: it affirmatively denies the ecclesial identification ('Christ needs no constructed body beneath Him'), which is a contradiction of the consensus core, not a boundary adjustment.","confidence":"high"}
